title: The Division of Labour and How Work Feels
text:
I want to trace one long change in how work is organised, because it explains a good deal about how people experience their jobs. Begin with the artisan workshop, where one worker understood the whole product and set the pace of making it. Then comes the division of labour, in which the task is broken into steps and each worker repeats one of them. Output rises sharply; the worker's relation to the product changes completely.

Durkheim saw in this the basis of a new kind of social bond. In small-scale societies, he argued, people are held together by similarity, since they do much the same work and share much the same outlook. In complex societies they are held together by difference, because each person depends on others precisely by not being self-sufficient. He called these mechanical and organic solidarity. Others found a cost in the same process. Marx described alienation, the separation of workers from the product, from the act of making, and from their own creative capacity. Braverman later argued that subdividing a job systematically strips skill and judgement from the shop floor and concentrates them in management. Both readings survive, which is why one reorganisation can be called efficiency by one researcher and deskilling by another.
points: Work moved from the artisan workshop, where one worker made the whole product, to a division of labour with repeated single steps.
The division of labour raises output but changes the worker's relation to the product.
Durkheim argued small societies are bound by similarity, which he called mechanical solidarity.
Complex societies are bound by interdependence between different specialists, which he called organic solidarity.
Marx described alienation from the product, the process and the worker's own creative capacity, and Braverman argued subdivided work removes skill to management.
The same reorganisation can therefore be described as efficiency or as deskilling.
